entry.definition: Needing or using a lot of physical or mental effort and energy.
entry.example: After her cast came off, the doctor told her to avoid strenuous exercise for two more weeks.
entry.nuance: Strenuous stresses the energy a task uses up, while arduous stresses how long and hard it is to get through. Don't confuse it with strident, which means harsh and loud.
entry.prompt: A hiking guide is describing the day's route to a group of visitors.
options: The last climb is strenuous, so rest and drink water before you start.
The flat, paved loop is so strenuous that toddlers stroll it in sandals.
The guide's strenuous voice grated on everyone's ears like a whistle.
From the summit, the view is strenuous, with soft colors fading into the valley.
reasons: A steep climb that calls for rest and water beforehand takes a lot of exertion.
An easy walk that small children can manage is the opposite of hard work.
A harsh, piercing voice is strident. The two words look alike but mean different things.
A view takes no effort to look at, so the word doesn't fit a pleasant scene.

practice.prompt: A family spends a Saturday moving into a new apartment.
options: The new kitchen smelled strenuous, like fresh paint and lemons.
Hauling the couch up four flights of stairs was the most strenuous job of the day.
Plugging in the lamp was strenuous, needing barely a flick of the wrist.
A neighbor's strenuous laugh cut sharply through the thin walls.
reasons: A smell doesn't use up energy, so the word has nothing to describe here.
Lifting heavy furniture up many stairs takes great physical effort.
A task that takes almost no effort can't be called exhausting.
A shrill, grating sound is strident, not effortful. This mixes up two look-alike words.
